A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UniLID research. All 14 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including appendices A-B and A-E respectively, are readable; their text, equations, figures and tables support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-identification experiments, including benchmark comparisons, dialect identification, sample-efficiency studies and vocabulary ablations in Tables 1-8 and Figure 1.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds original decoding, corruption, hyperparameter, timing and error-analysis results in Tables 9-18.

M1.justification: The default shared-vocabulary, per-language EM and Viterbi classification procedure remains unchanged. v2 adds limited experimental inference variants: exact marginalization in Appendix B.1 and length-normalized scoring in Appendix E.3. Neither replaces the default; the newly disclosed probability floor does not itself establish a change to the earlier implementation.

E1.justification: The six benchmark datasets and language-identification tasks are retained. Appendix B.2 adds a distinct input-corruption scenario using character replacements on WiLI at rates up to 50%. The script and resource breakdowns analyze the existing GlotLID-C population.

E2.justification: The fastText, CLD3 and GlotLID-M comparisons remain. Section 6 newly compares dialect-group scores with reported DSL-ML 2024 shared-task systems, including French macro-F1 of 0.534 versus 0.385. These additional comparators are unnamed, and reruns or matched evaluation splits are not documented.

E3.justification: The original splits and headline training budgets are retained, but the evaluation design expands substantially. Additions include DeepSeek3.2 and Qwen3 vocabulary configurations, a specified stochastic corruption protocol, fastText epoch/minimum-count sweeps, comparative timing on the same hardware, and a 500,000-sample normalization experiment with an unnormalized rescoring control.

E4.justification: v2 adds tests of Viterbi versus marginalization, character-noise robustness, fastText hyperparameter sensitivity, and performance by script and resource tier. It also investigates segmentation-length bias and tests whether length normalization helps. These substantially extend v1's sample-efficiency, input-length and vocabulary analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 1 and Table 6 retain identical mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting, without adding seed or repeated-run counts. v2 calls the marginalization gain statistically insignificant but supplies no identified test, interval or uncertainty-estimation procedure; this is an added result characterization rather than a documented statistical-method change.

E6.justification: Existing result rows in Tables 1-8 are retained, while additional tokenizer rows and Tables 9-18 substantially expand the findings. Examples include macro-F1 of 0.396 versus 0.678 for UniLID and fastText under 50% corruption, and accuracy falling from 0.960 to 0.885 with length normalization on the 500,000-sample subset. These are new comparisons, not improvements to the retained scores.

T1.justification: Section 4 corrects the inference complexity from O(|Lambda| + N*T_max) to O(|Lambda|*N*b + N*T_max), and corrects the maximum branching factor from N*T_max to T_max. It also adds complexity comparisons with fastText and CLD3. The underlying generative model and EM mathematics remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The main contribution and competitive-performance claims remain. The abstract and introduction replace 'surpassing 70%' with approximately 70%, and the introduction replaces exceeding 90% below 50 samples with approximately 90%, matching the retained results more closely. The introduction also removes the claim that additional language scoring effectively costs only O(|Lambda|).

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands explanations and applicability limits. It attributes low-data performance to vocabulary structure and generative modeling, recommends a broadly multilingual trained vocabulary over convenience reuse, and discusses weaknesses under heavy corruption, non-Latin scripts and very low-resource GlotLID-C conditions. New length-bias interpretations and proposed scaling remedies further extend the discussion.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies a 1e-12 token-probability floor, the selected fastText minimum-count setting, and 1,000 samples per language for base-tokenizer learning in the timing experiment. It also reports comparative training times. These improve implementation documentation without establishing changes to the earlier experiments; the code-release information is retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Ng and Jordan (2001) to support the generative-versus-discriminative sample-efficiency explanation and Ren et al. (2022) in the low-resource discussion. It also explicitly positions results against shared-task submissions. Most related work remains unchanged; the corrected Land and Pinter identifier is only a bibliographic correction.

P1.justification: The main sequence of Sections 1-8 remains intact. v2 makes targeted abstract and introduction edits, condenses dataset and baseline descriptions, revises parts of the results and discussion, and organizes additional analyses into appendix subsections. The new scientific content does not amount to a wholesale narrative reorganization.

P2.justification: Visual reporting expands substantially through Tables 9-18, covering decoding, corruption, tuning, timing and performance breakdowns. Tables 1 and 8 gain tokenizer rows. Figure 1 and the existing table structures are largely retained, while the new tables introduce substantial additional appendix layouts.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens validation: previously untested inference choices and unsupported comparative timing claims receive direct evidence, while new analyses expose important noise, script and length-related limitations. Corrected complexity and moderated sample-efficiency claims improve accuracy. Reporting remains imperfect: Section 6 gives GlotLID-C latency as 0.274 ms versus 0.307 ms in Table 12, and statistical insignificance is asserted without a stated test. These weaknesses limit individual conclusions but do not outweigh the substantial improvement in validation and characterization of applicability.
